Time is Not Compute: Scaling Laws for Wall-Clock Constrained Training on Consumer GPUs

Yi Liu Affiliation: Independent Researcher Email: lylewis@outlook.com
Abstract

Scaling laws relate model quality to compute budget (FLOPs), but practitioners face wall-clock time constraints, not compute budgets. We study optimal model sizing under fixed time budgets from 5 minutes to 24 hours on consumer GPUs (RTX 4090). Across 70+ runs spanning 50M–1031M parameters, we find: (1) at each time budget a U-shaped curve emerges where too-small models overfit and too-large models undertrain; (2) optimal model size follows N∗∝t0.60N^{*}\propto t^{0.60}, growing faster than Chinchilla’s N∗∝C0.50N^{*}\propto C^{0.50}, with α=0.60±0.07\alpha=0.60\pm 0.07 robustly exceeding compute-optimal across all sensitivity analyses; (3) a dual U-shape mechanism: short-budget U-curves arise from compute bottlenecks, while long-budget U-curves emerge from data bottlenecks (overfitting), with an intermediate regime where the U-curve temporarily disappears. These findings have immediate implications for researchers training on consumer hardware, where wall-clock time—not FLOPs—is the binding constraint. We release all code, logs, and 70+ experimental configurations.

1 Introduction

Motivation.

Scaling laws are among the most consequential empirical findings in deep learning. The seminal work of Kaplan et al. (2020) established smooth power-law relationships between model performance, model size, dataset size, and compute budget. Hoffmann et al. (2022) refined these into the widely-adopted Chinchilla prescription: for a compute budget CC (in FLOPs), the optimal model size scales as N∗∝C0.50N^{*}\propto C^{0.50}, and compute should be split roughly equally between model parameters and training tokens.

However, these laws share a critical assumption: the independent variable is compute (FLOPs). In practice, most researchers—especially those working on consumer hardware—think in wall-clock time, not FLOPs. The practitioner’s question is: “I have 4 hours on my RTX 4090. What size model should I train?” Chinchilla cannot directly answer this because it abstracts away a crucial factor: throughput.

The throughput gap.

Throughput varies dramatically across model sizes on fixed hardware. On an RTX 4090, a 50M-parameter model processes 428K tokens/second while a 519M-parameter model achieves only 36K—a 12×12\times gap. Under a fixed time budget, this means a small model sees far more training data. The compute-optimal allocation (Chinchilla) implicitly treats time and compute as interchangeable. They are not: doubling model size on fixed hardware does not double the compute consumed—it increases compute by only ∼\sim15% (because FLOPs ∝N\propto N but throughput ∝N−0.8\propto N^{-0.8}, yielding C∝N0.2⋅tC\propto N^{0.2}\cdot t).

This disconnect has practical consequences. A researcher following Chinchilla scaling on an RTX 4090 with a 4-hour budget would choose a model roughly C\sqrt{C} in size. But because throughput is non-linear, the time-optimal choice may differ substantially.

Contributions.

We study time-constrained scaling laws: given wall-clock budget tt on consumer hardware, what is the optimal model size N∗​(t)N^{*}(t)? We conduct 70+ training runs on 8×\times RTX 4090, spanning 50M–1031M parameters across 8 time budgets (5 minutes to 24 hours). Our key findings:

  1. 1.

    U-shaped optimality curves at every budget from 5min to 24h, where the optimal size monotonically shifts right as time increases: D8 (50M, 5min) →\to D10 (86M, 30min) →\to D14 (201M, 1h) →\to D16 (285M, 4h) →\to D20 (519M, 8h) →\to D24 (856M, 12h) →\to D26 (1031M, 24h).

  2. 2.

    Scaling exponent α=0.60±0.07\alpha=0.60\pm 0.07, robustly exceeding Chinchilla’s 0.50. The 95% confidence interval [0.53,0.67][0.53,0.67] excludes the compute-optimal value, demonstrating that time-constrained optimal sizing is a fundamentally different regime.

  3. 3.

    A dual U-shape mechanism: at short budgets (≤\leq8h), U-curves arise from compute bottlenecks—large models cannot process enough data. At long budgets (≥\geq24h), U-curves re-emerge from data bottlenecks—medium models overfit on the finite dataset. Between these regimes (∼\sim12h), the U-curve temporarily disappears as larger models improve monotonically.

  4. 4.

    Diminishing returns: L∗​(t)=1.22×t−0.061L^{*}(t)=1.22\times t^{-0.061} (R2=0.971R^{2}=0.971). The first 30 minutes yield 0.16 bpb improvement; hours 8–24 yield only 0.022 bpb combined.

Practical implication: doubling your time budget →\to increase model size by 1.52×1.52\times (20.602^{0.60}), compared to Chinchilla’s 1.41×1.41\times (20.502^{0.50}). Over a 10×10\times time increase, this means 3.98×3.98\times vs. 3.16×3.16\times model size—a 26% difference that compounds over longer budgets. We release all code and training logs to enable reproduction.

2 Related Work

Neural scaling laws.

Kaplan et al. (2020) established power-law scaling of language model loss with model size, dataset size, and compute. Their key finding—that larger models are more sample-efficient—underpins the trend toward ever-larger models. Hoffmann et al. (2022) (Chinchilla) refined this by showing that Kaplan et al. underestimated the importance of data: compute-optimal training requires roughly equal scaling of parameters and tokens, yielding N∗∝C0.50N^{*}\propto C^{0.50} and D∗∝C0.50D^{*}\propto C^{0.50}. Our work extends this framework by replacing compute CC with wall-clock time tt as the independent variable, finding N∗∝t0.60N^{*}\propto t^{0.60}.

Data-constrained scaling.

Muennighoff et al. (2023) studied the regime where training data is limited and must be repeated, showing that data repetition yields diminishing returns—a finding directly relevant to our setting, where small models exhaust the dataset and cycle through it many times. Hernandez et al. (2022) analyzed transfer learning scaling; Clark et al. (2022) proposed unified scaling laws incorporating model, data, and training steps.

Inference-optimal scaling.

Sardana and Frankle (2023) studied inference-optimal training, where the optimization target includes inference cost. Their setting resonates with ours: both deviate from pure compute-optimality by incorporating practical constraints. However, their constraint is inference cost per query, while ours is wall-clock training time.

Efficient training on consumer hardware.

Dettmers et al. (2023) enabled single-GPU fine-tuning via 4-bit quantization, dramatically lowering the barrier to LLM training. The autoresearch framework (Karpathy, 2025) provides small-scale pre-training pipelines for research. Dao et al. (2022) made attention O⁡(N)O(N) in memory, enabling longer sequences on limited VRAM. Our work operates in this ecosystem, studying pre-training scaling on consumer GPUs.

Architecture comparisons.

We compare Dense Transformers against MoE (Jiang et al., 2024; Dai et al., 2024), linear attention variants (RetNet (Sun et al., 2023), GLA (Yang et al., 2023), RWKV (Peng et al., 2023)), finding Dense Transformers with Flash Attention dominant under time constraints on consumer GPUs.

Batch size and training dynamics.

McCandlish et al. (2018) analyzed the critical batch size and its relation to compute–time trade-offs. Li and Gimpel (2024) studied the “loss surge” phenomenon during training. Our work complements these by providing a macro-level time–performance–size relationship.

3 Experimental Setup

3.1 Hardware and Software

Hardware.

We use a single server with 8×\times NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs (24GB VRAM each), an AMD EPYC 7542 32-core CPU, and 503GB RAM. Each GPU runs one independent training job—we do not use multi-GPU parallelism (data-parallel or model-parallel). This “embarrassingly parallel” setup maximizes experimental throughput: 8 configurations run simultaneously. The RTX 4090 represents the highest-end consumer GPU available in 2026, making our results directly relevant to the research community.

Software.

We use the autoresearch framework (Karpathy, 2025) with Flash Attention v2, torch.compile (mode=default, BF16 precision), and cosine learning rate schedule with warmup. All training uses a single-epoch paradigm where the learning rate decays to 10% of peak over the training budget, with 10% warmup steps.

3.2 Architecture Family

We use decoder-only Transformers with a single “DEPTH” parameter DD that controls all dimensions:

n​_​l​a​y​e​r​s=D,m​o​d​e​l​_​d​i​m=64​D,n​_​h​e​a​d​s=D,h​e​a​d​_​d​i​m=64n\_layers=D,\quad model\_dim=64D,\quad n\_heads=D,\quad head\_dim=64 (1)

This parameterization ensures constant architectural ratios across scales: the aspect ratio (width/depth) is always 64, and the number of attention heads equals the depth. This eliminates confounding variables from architectural choices and isolates the effect of scale.

Table 3 in the Appendix shows all configurations. Key data points: D8 has 50.3M parameters with throughput 428K tok/sec; D14 has 200.9M at 110K tok/sec; D20 has 519.0M at 36K tok/sec; D26 has ∼\sim1031M at ∼\sim5K tok/sec. This 85×85\times throughput range across our model family is precisely what drives the divergence between time-constrained and compute-constrained scaling.

3.3 Dataset

We use FineWeb-Edu (Penedo et al., 2024), a curated web corpus, tokenized with BPE (32K vocabulary). Our training set contains ∼\sim48M tokens. This deliberately small dataset enables studying the capacity–data–overfitting interplay: small models exhaust the data rapidly (D8 cycles through 250+ times at 12h), while large models (D26 at 24h) see fewer than 3 epochs. We report validation bits-per-byte (BPB) throughout.

Why a small dataset?

While larger datasets would avoid overfitting, our small dataset serves a crucial purpose: it creates a natural laboratory for studying both forms of suboptimality simultaneously—undertrained large models and overfit small models—within practical time budgets. With a sufficiently large dataset, the U-curve’s left limb (overfitting) would not appear until much longer training, making the phenomenon harder to observe.

3.4 Experimental Design

We train models across 8 time budgets: 5 minutes, 30 minutes, 1 hour, 2 hours, 4 hours, 8 hours, 12 hours, and 24 hours. At each budget, we run 4–8 model sizes in parallel across GPUs. All configurations share identical hyperparameters (learning rate 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, batch size 64 sequences of 512 tokens) except DEPTH and cases where large models require reduced batch size for VRAM constraints (D26 uses batch size 1). Learning rate ablations (Section 4.5) confirm robustness to this choice.

In total, we conduct 70+ individual training runs, spanning a 20×20\times parameter range (50M–1031M) and a 288×288\times time range (5min–24h).

4 Results

4.1 U-Shaped Optimality at Every Time Budget

Our central empirical finding is that at every time budget, validation BPB versus model size yields a characteristic U-shaped curve. Table 1 presents complete results across all 8 time budgets and 10 model sizes.

The U-shape arises from two competing forces. The left limb (too-small models): these models exhaust the training data and overfit. D8 at 4h achieves BPB 0.925, worse than its 2h result of 0.906; by 12h, its BPB degrades further to 0.919 after cycling through the 48M-token dataset over 250 times. The right limb (too-large models): insufficient throughput means too little data is processed to utilize model capacity—D24 at 5min sees only 13M tokens, yielding BPB 1.854, far worse than D8’s 1.133 with 134M tokens.

The optimal model shifts right monotonically with time: D8 (5min) →\to D10 (30min) →\to D14 (1h) →\to D14=D16 (2h) →\to D16 (4h) →\to D20 (8h) →\to D24 (12h) →\to D26 (24h). This monotonic rightward shift is the key empirical regularity that enables fitting a scaling law.

4.2 Time-Constrained Scaling Law

Fitting a power law N∗​(t)=a⋅tαN^{*}(t)=a\cdot t^{\alpha} to all 8 time points (5min–24h):

N∗​(t)=14.20×t0.595(R2=0.963)N^{*}(t)=14.20\times t^{0.595}\quad(R^{2}=0.963) (2)

where N∗N^{*} is optimal parameters (millions) and tt is time (minutes). The exponent α=0.595±0.067\alpha=0.595\pm 0.067 exceeds Chinchilla’s compute-optimal exponent of 0.50 by approximately 20%.

Statistical significance.

The 95% confidence interval for α\alpha is [0.53,0.67][0.53,0.67], which excludes the Chinchilla value of 0.50. This confirms that time-constrained scaling represents a genuinely different regime from compute-constrained scaling.

Practical interpretation.

Doubling the time budget prescribes 20.60=1.52×2^{0.60}=1.52\times the model size, compared to Chinchilla’s 20.50=1.41×2^{0.50}=1.41\times. Over a 10×10\times increase, this means 3.98×3.98\times vs. 3.16×3.16\times model size. The difference compounds: for a researcher moving from a 1-hour “quick experiment” to a 24-hour overnight run, our law recommends a 240.60/10.60=7.2×24^{0.60}/1^{0.60}=7.2\times larger model, vs. Chinchilla’s 240.50=4.9×24^{0.50}=4.9\times.

Depth scaling.

The optimal DEPTH also follows a power law: D∗​(t)=4.97×t0.231D^{*}(t)=4.97\times t^{0.231} (R2=0.958R^{2}=0.958).

Sensitivity analysis.

We verify robustness by varying fitting choices (full results in Table 4, Appendix). At 2h, D14 and D16 tie at BPB 0.901; we test using average (243M), D16 only, D14 only, and excluding the 2h point. Across all variants, α\alpha robustly exceeds 0.50 (α∈[0.60,0.81]\alpha\in[0.60,0.81]). Notably, α\alpha decreased from 0.747 (7 points) to 0.595 (8 points) upon adding 24h data. We discuss this convergence behavior in Section 5.

4.3 Loss Scaling

The best achievable loss at each time budget follows:

L∗​(t)=1.223×t−0.061(R2=0.971)L^{*}(t)=1.223\times t^{-0.061}\quad(R^{2}=0.971) (3)

Diminishing returns are pronounced (full breakdown in Table 5, Appendix): the first 30 minutes yield 0.16 bpb improvement (0.38 bpb/hour), while hours 8–24 yield only 0.022 bpb combined (0.001 bpb/hour). On consumer GPUs with limited data, the first hour captures the majority of achievable improvement—quick exploratory runs (1–4h) provide most of the signal.

4.4 The Dual U-Shape: Two Bottlenecks, One Curve

A striking finding from our 24h experiments is the emergence of a second U-shape driven by a completely different mechanism than the first.

Short-budget U-shape (5min–8h): compute bottleneck.

At budgets ≤\leq8h, the right limb of the U-curve arises because large models have insufficient throughput to process enough data. D24 (856M) at 4h achieves BPB 0.896—far from its potential—because it processes only ∼\sim13M tokens.

U-curve disappearance (∼\sim12h): transitional regime.

At 12h, a remarkable phenomenon occurs: the U-curve disappears. BPB decreases monotonically from D10 (0.885) to D24 (0.824). The largest model shows the most dramatic improvement (Δ8​h→12​h=−0.021\Delta_{8h\to 12h}=-0.021), suggesting the true optimum exceeds our VRAM capacity.

Long-budget U-shape (24h): data bottleneck.

At 24h, the U-curve returns—but its left limb has a new cause. Medium models (D14–D20), which were optimal at shorter budgets, now overfit: D14’s BPB degrades from 0.852 (12h) to 0.857 (24h); D18 degrades from 0.833 to 0.845 (+0.012). Only D24 and D26 continue improving (see Table 6 in Appendix for full breakdown). The U-curve’s left limb at 24h is driven by data repetition, not insufficient compute.

This dual U-shape mechanism means the “safe zone” of near-optimal model sizes narrows at long budgets: at 4h, D14–D18 all achieve within 0.004 of optimal; at 24h, only D24–D26 avoid overfitting.

4.5 Ablation Studies

Learning rate sensitivity.

We conduct LR ablations at two model sizes (D8 and D14) with 1h training, testing LR values from 1.5×10−41.5\times 10^{-4} to 6×10−46\times 10^{-4}. D14’s default LR (3×10−43\times 10^{-4}) is near-optimal, within 0.001 BPB of the best LR (6×10−46\times 10^{-4}, BPB 0.944 vs. 0.945). Even with optimal LR, D8 (BPB 0.948) does not beat D14 (0.945), confirming that the scaling law is robust to moderate LR variation.

Multi-seed validation.

We run 3 seeds (42, 123, 456) for four model sizes (D8, D10, D14, D16) at 30 minutes (Table 2). The results are remarkably stable: inter-seed standard deviation is at most 0.0032 BPB, while inter-model gaps reach 0.056 BPB—a factor of 17×17\times larger. The coefficient of variation is below 0.31% for all models. Crucially, D10 remains the optimal model at 30min across all seeds (mean=0.9734±0.0004\text{mean}=0.9734\pm 0.0004), and every D10 seed beats every D8 seed, confirming the Chinchilla crossover is robust to randomness. These results validate that our primary single-seed results are representative of the underlying trends.

Multi-architecture comparison.

At 5min on RTX 4090, we compare Dense Transformer against four alternatives: MoE (64 experts, top-1, fine-grained), RetNet with FLA Triton kernels, GLA with FLA kernels, and RWKV6 with FLA kernels. Results: Dense Transformer (1.133) ≫\gg MoE (1.143) ≫\gg RetNet (2.216) >> GLA (2.249) >> RWKV6 (2.258). Linear attention variants underperform by nearly 2×2\times despite achieving higher model FLOPs utilization (MFU: 20–27% vs. 10% for Dense). The architectural comparison justifies our focus on Dense Transformers.

5 Discussion

5.1 Why Time ≠\neq Compute

The mathematical origin of the time–compute divergence is straightforward. For a model of size NN trained for time tt, the compute consumed is:

C⁡(N,t)=6​N×τ⁡(N)×tC(N,t)=6N\times\tau(N)\times t (4)

where τ⁡(N)\tau(N) is throughput (tokens/second) and the factor 6 accounts for forward and backward passes. We empirically measure τ⁡(N)∝N−0.8\tau(N)\propto N^{-0.8} on our hardware (Table 3), giving:

C∝N×N−0.8×t=N0.2×tC\propto N\times N^{-0.8}\times t=N^{0.2}\times t (5)

Under compute constraints (fixed CC), doubling NN halves the available tokens: T=C/6​NT=C/6N. The penalty for increasing model size is direct and linear. Under time constraints (fixed tt), doubling NN reduces tokens by only 20.8≈1.74×2^{0.8}\approx 1.74\times: T=τ⁡(N)×tT=\tau(N)\times t. The penalty is indirect, mediated through throughput, and sublinear. This weaker penalty means time constraints favor larger models than compute constraints—precisely what α=0.60>0.50\alpha=0.60>0.50 captures.

5.2 Comparison with Chinchilla

The quantitative implications of α=0.60\alpha=0.60 vs. 0.50 compound with longer budgets. Doubling time prescribes 1.52×1.52\times the model (vs. Chinchilla’s 1.41×1.41\times); over a 10×10\times increase: 3.98×3.98\times vs. 3.16×3.16\times; for the common scenario of scaling from 1h to 24h: 7.2×7.2\times vs. 4.9×4.9\times (Table 7 in Appendix).

The mechanism behind this divergence is the data repetition penalty. Under time constraints, small models process the same data many more times, suffering compounding repetition losses (Muennighoff et al., 2023). This creates a “push” toward larger models that is absent in compute-constrained settings with unlimited data.

5.3 Evolution of α\alpha

An intriguing phenomenon is the non-monotonic convergence of α\alpha as we add longer time points:

  • •

    5 points (5min–4h): α=0.44\alpha=0.44 — below Chinchilla

  • •

    6 points (+8h): α=0.55\alpha=0.55 — just above Chinchilla

  • •

    7 points (+12h): α=0.75\alpha=0.75 — far above Chinchilla

  • •

    8 points (+24h): α=0.60\alpha=0.60 — settled above Chinchilla

The 7-point estimate (α=0.75\alpha=0.75) was inflated because 12h was the first budget where the U-curve disappeared and D24 (the largest model) became optimal—this created an outsized leverage point. Adding 24h data with D26 (1031M) as the new optimum “pulled back” α\alpha to a more moderate 0.60. We believe α≈0.60\alpha\approx 0.60 is a reasonable estimate, though it may continue to evolve with even longer budgets.

The fact that α\alpha oscillates rather than converges monotonically suggests the relationship between N∗N^{*} and tt may not be a pure power law over all time scales. The dual U-shape mechanism (Section 4.4) introduces regime transitions that a single power law cannot perfectly capture. Nevertheless, R2=0.963R^{2}=0.963 indicates an excellent fit over our observed range.

5.4 The Disappearing and Returning U-Curve

The lifecycle of the U-curve across time budgets reveals three distinct regimes:

Regime 1: Compute-bounded (5min–8h). U-curves with clear minima. The right limb arises from throughput limitations. Optimal model sizes are well below VRAM capacity.

Regime 2: Transitional (∼\sim12h). The U-curve vanishes: BPB decreases monotonically with model size. This represents the “sweet spot” where even the largest fittable model (D24, 856M) benefits from additional training without overfitting. The true optimum likely exceeds single-GPU VRAM—a natural transition point to multi-GPU training.

Regime 3: Data-bounded (≥\geq24h). The U-curve returns, but with inverted causation: the left limb is now driven by overfitting (too many epochs on finite data), not insufficient compute. Models D14–D20 degrade from their 12h BPBs. This regime is specific to finite datasets and would shift rightward with larger data.

This three-regime structure has a practical implication: there exists a “golden duration” for each dataset size beyond which increasing training time requires either more data or model scale beyond single-GPU capacity.

5.5 Practical Guidelines

Rule of thumb: double your time →\to 1.52×1.52\times model size (20.602^{0.60}). For exploratory work, 1–4 hours captures 80%+ of achievable improvement. For overnight runs (12–24h), maximize model size within VRAM constraints. Table 8 (Appendix) provides specific recommendations per time budget for RTX 4090.

5.6 Limitations

Our study has several limitations that future work should address:

  1. 1.

    Single GPU type. RTX 4090 has specific throughput–size scaling. A100/H100 GPUs may yield different α\alpha due to different memory bandwidth, compute ratios, and multi-GPU interconnects.

  2. 2.

    Small dataset. Our 48M-token dataset amplifies data repetition effects. With larger datasets (billions of tokens), the data-bounded regime (Section 4.4) would shift rightward, potentially reducing α\alpha toward 0.50.

  3. 3.

    Single architecture. While we confirm Dense Transformers dominate alternatives on consumer GPUs, the specific α\alpha value may differ for other architectures.

  4. 4.

    Limited multi-seed coverage. While our multi-seed experiment at 30 minutes confirms negligible inter-seed variance (σ<0.003\sigma<0.003), full multi-seed validation at all 8 time budgets would further strengthen confidence intervals, particularly at the longer budgets (12–24h) where single runs are expensive.

  5. 5.

    No multi-GPU training. At 12–24h, the optimal model approaches or exceeds single-GPU VRAM, suggesting multi-GPU training is necessary for longer budgets. The scaling law may behave differently in the multi-GPU regime due to communication overhead.

6 Conclusion

We introduce time-constrained scaling laws for language model training on consumer GPUs. Our central finding is that optimal model size scales as N∗​(t)∝t0.60N^{*}(t)\propto t^{0.60}, exceeding Chinchilla’s compute-optimal exponent of 0.50. This divergence arises from sublinear throughput scaling (τ∝N−0.8\tau\propto N^{-0.8}), which breaks the equivalence between time and compute as optimization targets.

Three key phenomena emerge from our 70+ training runs:

  1. 1.

    U-shaped optimality curves at every time budget, with the optimal model size monotonically shifting rightward from 50M (5min) to 1031M (24h).

  2. 2.

    A dual U-shape mechanism: short-budget U-curves from compute bottlenecks, long-budget U-curves from data bottlenecks, with a transitional regime where the U-curve disappears.

  3. 3.

    Severe diminishing returns: the first hour captures most achievable improvement; extending from 8h to 24h yields only 0.022 BPB—a finding that should inform how researchers allocate GPU time.

Most practitioners operate under time constraints, not compute budgets. Guidance in wall-clock hours—not teraFLOPs—makes scaling laws more actionable for the research community.

Broader impact.

Our findings suggest that the “bigger is better” narrative, while correct directionally, overstates the benefit of model scale under time constraints. For the growing community of researchers training on consumer hardware, understanding time-constrained scaling can save thousands of GPU-hours of misallocated compute.

Future work.

Natural extensions include: (1) multi-GPU training at 12h+ budgets, where the optimal model exceeds single-GPU VRAM; (2) datacenter GPUs (A100/H100) with different throughput profiles; (3) larger datasets to isolate throughput effects from data repetition; (4) testing whether α\alpha converges to a stable value with more time points; and (5) extending to fine-tuning and RLHF stages of the LLM pipeline.

Appendix G Multi-Seed Validation Details

The multi-seed experiment serves as a critical robustness check. At the 30-minute budget—where D10 (86M) and D8 (50M) are separated by only 0.002 BPB—all three D10 seeds produce lower BPB than all three D8 seeds. This pairwise dominance across 3×3=93\times 3=9 comparisons gives strong evidence that the Chinchilla crossover at 30 minutes is a genuine phenomenon, not a statistical artifact.

The exceptionally low variance of D10 (σ=0.0004\sigma=0.0004) compared to D14 and D16 (σ≈0.003\sigma\approx 0.003) likely reflects that D10 at 30min is operating at a natural “sweet spot” where it has processed sufficient data (∼\sim450M tokens, ∼\sim5×\times the dataset) to produce stable representations, whereas D14 and D16 have seen fewer tokens relative to their capacity and are thus more sensitive to initialization.
